newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission stalls on media concentration.
newsitem.headline: Commission stalls on media concentration.

text.p: The draft directive on media concentration will not be discussed at the European Commission's meeting on Wednesday, a Commission spokesman said on Tuesday.
Commission officials said that Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti had taken a personal decision not to put the plan on the agenda for this week's meeting.
That would give him time to reconsider the plan as Commissioners' aides appeared to prefer a recommendation, rather than a binding directive, they said.
The Commission had planned to hold an orientation debate on the draft directive in Strasbourg last week, but ran out of time.

Now, aware that a majority of Commissioners is uneasy about proposing something binding, Monti is taking his time before putting it on the agenda again, and the discussion could now take place after Easter.

External Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan is standing out against any form of EU intervention outside competition law to counter overconcentration of the media, while Culture Commissioner Marcelino Oreja wants something less binding than a directive.
The Commissioners are also aware of intense lobbying from industry.
On Tuesday Britain's Independent Television (ITV) said it feared the consequences if the Commission proposed a binding directive.

Under the plan -- drawn up in response to European Parliament demands for a binding directive to protect pluralism and democracy -- television stations would not be able to extend their market when they hold 30 percent of the audience in the zone of reception, be it national or regional.
The threshold, still subject to review, would be 10 percent on average for those involved in television, radio and newspapers.
ITV said it already clocks up 40 percent of the audience in its area of reception.
"The difficulty we face is that the TV companies almost all exceed the 30 percent audience share limit in their respective regions," said Barry Cox, Director of the ITV Association.

"So no matter how small they are in total UK audience terms, there is a real danger that they would not be able to grow their business locally. They may also be prevented from acquiring control of a broadcaster with over 30 percent audience share in another member state."

As the Commission plan takes shape ITV and other media interests are focusing on securing exemptions from the plan, but remain sceptical as even if an exemption is proposed, it might not survive the EU's complicated and lengthy legislative process which can end in conciliation with the Parliament.
